sections.heading: Coming close to the great God
sections.text: God, you are greater than I can take in. I come to you with reverence, but not with fear that drives me away. You stoop down to welcome people like me, and your kindness does not lessen your glory—it shows it. I have no claim on you. I am unworthy, but you invite me in. I am guilty, but you are full of mercy. I am needy, but your riches are beyond measure.
theological_themes: God is majestic and holy, yet merciful and near to the humble.
The believer approaches God with both reverent fear and real confidence because God welcomes sinners by grace.

scripture_references.connection: This passage grounds the believer's confidence to come near to God, not in personal worthiness, but in the mercy and help given through Christ our high priest.
God is described as exalted and holy, yet also as dwelling with the contrite and lowly. That combination supports the prayer’s movement of reverence joined with confidence.

sections.heading: Resting my hope on what you have given in Christ
sections.text: You have shown me compassion beyond measure by giving your own Son and not holding him back. Since you have given me Christ, I can trust you for everything I truly need in him. He is the ground under my hope, the safe place I run to, and the open way into your presence. Through him, show me my sin honestly, break my pride, and bring me to the end of trusting myself, so that the gospel becomes more precious to me.
theological_themes: God’s greatest mercy is the gift of his Son for sinners.
Christ is the foundation of hope and the way into God’s presence.
True conviction of sin and self-despair make the grace of the gospel dearer, not less necessary.

scripture_references.connection: Paul reasons from the Father’s gift of his Son to the believer’s confidence that God will graciously provide all that is needed in Christ.
This passage identifies Jesus’ sacrifice as the new and living way into God’s presence, matching the prayer’s confidence that access to God rests on Christ.
Paul distinguishes godly grief from despairing worldly sorrow. The prayer asks for conviction and brokenness that lead toward salvation and deeper love for the gospel.

sections.heading: Remembering the safety of belonging to Christ
sections.text: How blessed are those who belong to Jesus. In him they are at peace with you, cleared of every charge that could condemn them, rescued from the wrath to come, and made heirs of a glory still ahead. Let me live in that same hope—not lightly, but gratefully and securely, because my salvation rests in him.
theological_themes: Union with Christ brings peace with God, justification, rescue from judgment, and inheritance of future glory.
Christian confidence is secure because it rests on Christ rather than self.

scripture_references.connection: Paul links justification by faith with peace with God and access into grace, which directly supports the prayer’s confidence in Christ.
This passage speaks of believers waiting for the risen Son who delivers them from the wrath to come, echoing the prayer’s hope of rescue through Christ.
The Spirit bears witness that believers are God’s children and heirs with Christ, grounding the prayer’s language of future glory.

sections.heading: Asking for a life that shows your saving work
sections.text: Give me a heart that is less captivated by the world, more deeply in love with the Savior, more committed to your people, and more ready for your service. Let these things show—not as a way to earn salvation, but as evidence that your saving grace is truly at work in me.
theological_themes: Saving grace changes a person’s loves, loyalties, and service.
Love for Christ, detachment from the world, commitment to the church, and obedience are fruits of salvation, not the basis of it.

scripture_references.connection: John warns against loving the world’s passing desires, which supports the prayer’s request for the world to lose its grip on the heart.
Grace not only saves but trains believers to renounce ungodliness and become zealous for good works. This fits the prayer’s request for visible evidence of salvation.
The call to meet together and stir one another up to love and good works supports the prayer’s desire for attachment to God’s house and people.

sections.heading: Letting my life point others to Jesus
sections.text: Let my character and my daily choices leave a serious, winsome impression on the people around me. Make my life honest enough, humble enough, and kind enough that others would be drawn to ask about the way to my Master.
theological_themes: A believer’s conduct should bear witness to Christ.
Godly character can make the gospel visible and invite others toward the Lord.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that the visible good works of his people should lead others to glorify the Father, which supports the prayer’s desire for a life that points beyond itself.
Peter connects honorable conduct before outsiders with God being glorified, grounding the prayer’s concern that daily behavior would make a faithful impression.

sections.heading: Depending on you in everything you send
sections.text: Do not let anything that happens to me—whether pleasant or painful—damage the life of my soul. Instead, use every circumstance to deepen me, steady me, and draw me nearer to you. Send me your help. The duties, opportunities, and means you give me are not meant to make me self-sufficient. Even the best plans, habits, and efforts will come to nothing unless you add your blessing.
theological_themes: God can use both joys and hardships for spiritual growth.
Believers remain dependent on God even when using the means and opportunities he provides.
Human effort and faithful means need God’s blessing to bear lasting fruit.

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that trials can produce steadfastness and maturity, supporting the prayer’s request that painful events would increase rather than harm spiritual prosperity.
Jesus teaches that fruitfulness depends on abiding in him and that apart from him his disciples can do nothing, matching the prayer’s rejection of self-sufficiency.
Paul distinguishes human planting and watering from God giving growth, which supports the prayer’s confession that even good means are vain without God’s blessing.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase about being 'justified from all things' and 'delivered from coming wrath' reflects a strongly Reformed evangelical understanding of salvation and final judgment. I preserved this rather than softening it.

The original asks for evidences that 'prove' the person is a subject of salvation. To avoid implying works-based salvation, the adaptation states that these fruits do not earn salvation but show God’s saving grace at work.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered 'thy condescension equals thy grandeur, and thy goodness is thy glory' as God stooping down to welcome sinners and showing his glory through kindness, because the original joins divine majesty with merciful nearness.
I interpreted 'attachment to his house' as commitment to God’s gathered people and worship rather than attachment to a church building as such.
I rendered 'deadness to the world' as the world’s approval and rewards losing their grip, preserving the Puritan concern without implying hatred of creation or ordinary earthly responsibilities.
I took 'best means will be vain without super-added blessings' to mean that spiritual disciplines, duties, and opportunities are good but ineffective for lasting fruit unless God blesses them.
